claim: You can integrate an Application Load Balancer with AWS WAF, whose rules on IP addresses, HTTP headers and URI strings can block, allow or count web requests.
q: Can AWS WAF protect an Application Load Balancer, and what can its rules do?
values: block, allow, or monitor (count) web requests
note: d110. The ELB guides and the WAF resource list name no Network Load Balancer for AWS WAF; the WAF regional resource list in docs/waf/latest/developerguide/how-aws-waf-works-resources lists Application Load Balancer and no Network Load Balancer (absence, not a sentence).
ev: www/elasticloadbalancing/faqs

You can integrate your Application Load Balancer with AWS Web Application Firewall (WAF), a web application firewall that helps protect web applications from attacks by allowing you to configure rules based on IP addresses, HTTP headers, and custom uniform resource identifier (URI) strings.
www/elasticloadbalancing/faqs
Using these rules, AWS WAF can block, allow, or monitor (count) web requests for your web application.

claim: CloudFront VPC origins let CloudFront deliver content from Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers and EC2 instances in private subnets, so the origins need no public access.
q: Can CloudFront use a load balancer in a private subnet as its origin, and which types?
values: Application Load Balancers (ALBs), Network Load Balancers (NLBs)
in private subnets as VPC origins
private subnets with no public access
ev: docs/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-vpc-origins
You can use Application Load Balancers (ALBs), Network Load Balancers (NLBs), and EC2 instances in private subnets as VPC origins.
docs/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-vpc-origins
You can move your origins to private subnets with no public access, and you don’t have to implement access control lists (ACLs) or other mechanisms to restrict access to your origins.

scope: AWS Well-Architected Framework, security pillar SEC09-BP02
ev: docs/wellarchitected/latest/security-pillar/sec_protect_data_transit_encrypt
Your defined encryption requirements should be based on the latest standards and best practices and only allow secure protocols.
docs/wellarchitected/latest/security-pillar/sec_protect_data_transit_encrypt

claim: AWS recommends the post-quantum TLS security policy ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-PQ-2025-09, or its FIPS version, for load balancer listeners.
q: Which TLS security policy does AWS recommend for an Application Load Balancer HTTPS listener?
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/describe-ssl-policies
AWS recommends implementing the new post-quantum TLS (PQ-TLS) based security policy  `ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-PQ-2025-09` or `ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-FIPS-PQ-2025-09`.

claim: An Application Load Balancer can verify JSON Web Tokens (JWT) that clients send for service-to-service or machine-to-machine communication, and rejects the request when the token is not valid.
q: Can an Application Load Balancer validate machine-to-machine access tokens?
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/listener-verify-jwt
You can configure an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to verify JSON Web Tokens (JWT) provided by clients for secure service-to-service (S2S) or machine-to-machine (M2M) communications.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/listener-verify-jwt
If the token is valid, the load balancer forwards the request with token as is to the target. Otherwise, it rejects the request.

claim: An Application Load Balancer rule transform rewrites the host header or the URL of a request before it is routed to targets; the rewrite does not change the routing decision.
q: Can an Application Load Balancer rewrite the URL or host header of a request?
values: rewrites inbound requests before they are routed
does not change the routing decision
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/rule-transforms
A rule transform rewrites inbound requests before they are routed to targets.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/rule-transforms
Rewriting a request does not change the routing decision made when evaluating the rule conditions.

claim: An Application Load Balancer can modify HTTP request and response headers without changes to the application code.
q: Can an Application Load Balancer change HTTP headers without application code changes?
values: for both request and response headers
Without having to update your application code
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/header-modification
HTTP header modification is supported by Application Load Balancers, for both request and response headers.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/header-modification
Without having to update your application code, header modification allows you more control over your application's traffic and security.

claim: An LCU reservation reserves a static minimum capacity for a load balancer, for example before an event with a sudden, unusually high traffic spike; the load balancer still scales up and down above that minimum.
q: How do you make sure a load balancer can absorb a planned traffic spike, such as a launch event?
values: an upcoming event that will have a sudden
scope: Application, Network and Gateway Load Balancers
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/capacity-unit-reservation
Load balancer Capacity Unit (LCU) reservations allow you to reserve a static minimum capacity for your load balancer.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/capacity-unit-reservation

When minimum capacity is configured, your load balancer continues scaling up or down based on the traffic received, but also prevents the capacity from going lower than the minimum capacity configured.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/capacity-unit-reservation
You have an upcoming event that will have a sudden, unusual high traffic and want to ensure your load balancer can support the sudden traffic spike during the event.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/gateway/capacity-unit-reservation
Load balancer Capacity Unit (LCU) reservations allow you to reserve a static minimum capacity for your load balancer.

claim: AWS calls a centralized session management data store the ideal solution for HTTP sessions in modern architectures: it gives consistent user experiences across all web servers and better session durability when the web server fleet is elastic.
q: Where does AWS suggest keeping HTTP session data when web servers scale in and out?
values: when your fleet of web servers is elastic
scope: web applications behind a load balancer
note: d113. Links to elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what, elb-sticky-uneven-load-nat and ec2-auto-scaling-wa-offload-session-data; ElastiCache detail belongs to its own chapter.
ev: www/caching/session-management

With modern application architectures, utilizing a centralized session management data store is the ideal solution for a number of reasons including providing, consistent user experiences across all web servers, better session durability when your fleet of web servers is elastic and higher availability when session data is replicated across cache servers.

claim: Application Load Balancer sticky sessions are useful for servers that keep state information; the client must support cookies.
q: When are Application Load Balancer sticky sessions useful, and what do clients need?
ev: docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes
This feature is useful for servers that maintain state information in order to provide a continuous experience to clients.
docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes
To use sticky sessions, the client must support cookies.
